title: TOEFL Reading 2026: The Three New Task Types
summary: What Complete the Words, Read in Daily Life and Read an Academic Passage actually ask you to do — and how the two-stage adaptive section works.

nodes.label: Complete the Words
nodes.note: Fill in missing letters in key words

nodes.label: Two-stage adaptive
nodes.note: Difficulty shifts after the first stage

chunks.heading: Complete the Words — vocabulary in context
chunks.body: You see a short text with **letters missing from key words** and complete them. It rewards a strong vocabulary and accurate **spelling** in context, read quickly.
chunks.realExample: You might see: 'Students must ret_rn library books before the end of te_m.' You complete 'return' and 'term'. The surrounding sentence tells you the word; you supply the spelling.
chunks.memoryHook: Read the whole sentence first — the context hands you the word, you just spell it.

chunks.heading: Read in Daily Life — everyday English
chunks.body: You read **brief, practical texts** — notices, messages, short informational texts — and answer comprehension questions. This is real-world reading, not academic prose.
chunks.realExample: A dorm notice: 'The laundry room on Floor 2 is closed for repairs; please use Floor 4 until Monday.' A question might ask where students should do laundry this week.
chunks.memoryHook: Skim for the practical point: what changed, who's affected, what to do.

chunks.heading: Read an Academic Passage — the university text
chunks.body: You read a **short academic passage**, similar to what you'd meet in a university course, and answer questions on main ideas and details. Shorter than the old TOEFL passages, but the academic reading skills are the same.
chunks.realExample: A passage on why coral reefs bleach: a question tests the main cause, another tests a specific detail. Locate the sentence that answers it rather than re-reading the whole text.
chunks.memoryHook: Find the sentence, not the whole passage. Questions point to a spot.

chunks.heading: It's adaptive — do your best early
chunks.body: Reading is **two-stage adaptive**: your performance in the first stage sets the difficulty of the second. So **give the early items your full focus** — they steer the rest of the section.
chunks.realExample: If items start feeling harder in the second stage, that's usually a good sign — the test raised the level because you handled stage one well. Don't panic; keep going.
chunks.memoryHook: Harder second half? That often means you're doing well. Strong start = higher ceiling.

recall.q: What does the 'Complete the Words' task ask you to do?
recall.a: Fill in letters missing from key words in a short text — it tests vocabulary and spelling in context.

recall.q: What kind of texts appear in 'Read in Daily Life'?
recall.a: Brief practical texts such as notices, messages and short informational texts, with comprehension questions.

recall.q: How does the 'Read an Academic Passage' task compare to the old TOEFL reading?
recall.a: It's a shorter university-style passage with questions, but it tests the same academic reading skills as before.

recall.q: How does the two-stage adaptive Reading section work?
recall.a: Your performance in the first stage sets the difficulty of the second stage, so early items matter.

recall.q: Why might questions feel harder in the second stage?
recall.a: Because you did well in the first stage and the test raised the difficulty — it's usually a positive sign.
